segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The gap in the Kettle Row wall was a shoulder wide and no more, and it took Jory Brennick two tries to get through it. He went in with both arms ahead of him and the stone dragging along his ribs. Something caught at his belt. He kicked once, felt it give, and was through into water so black he had to hold still until his eyes found the green smear of daylight behind him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora Quill came after, smaller and smarter about it, and turned a slow circle beside him with her hand out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was a back room, a long one. Silt stood up off the floor in clouds where their feet went near it, so they swam high, close to a ceiling that had sagged but held. The far wall had a bench along the whole length of it, and the bench was not empty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Glass. Rows of it, racked and fallen and cracked across, bellied vessels with long necks, flat dishes, a jar with its stopper still seated. Between them lay iron gone to orange lumps that had been tools once. A stone mortar sat at the end of the bench, and it was the size of a wash basin, and it had not moved since the water came. Nobody kept that in a house cellar. Nobody kept that anywhere but a working room.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora found the post first. It ran floor to ceiling, a squared oak beam holding the sag out of the boards above, and bolted to it at chest height was a strongbox the size of a bread crock.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory got close before he saw the wall beside it. The stone there was scarred — four or five short bites of a chisel, the edges square, the colour of fresh-broken grey. Everything else in that room wore twenty years of weed and soft brown fur. These cuts wore nothing at all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He put his glove on the strongbox lid and worked round to the lock plate. There was no keyhole. There was no slot, no hasp, no shackle. Only a plate of something darker than iron with letters standing proud of it, cut deep and spaced out like a name said slowly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And it was warm. Through a wet glove, in water cold enough to ache in the jaw, it was warm, the way the back of a dog is warm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory took his hand away. His chest had started to pull. Liora was already at his elbow with two fingers raised, pointing up, and she did not wait to see whether he followed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came up ten feet apart and Maud Brennick had the boat between them before either had finished the first breath. Liora got the gunwale and hung there, blowing.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: Somebody's been cutting at that wall.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Four marks. Five. Right alongside the box, and clean as a quarry face.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: How clean?

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: No growth on them. Nothing on them. Everything else down there has a beard.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud sat back on the thwart and looked at the water as if it owed her an explanation.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Weed takes hold inside a season on bare stone. I've watched it do it. Anything cut before midsummer would be furred by now.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: So it was cut after midsummer.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: By who? The old man's only had the letter a month and he can't swim a stroke. Nobody dives Kettle Row. There's nothing in it but dyers' vats.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: There's a box bolted to a post in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory hauled himself over the side and sat dripping with his arms on his knees. He could still feel the warmth of that plate in the palm of his glove, which made no sense at all, the water being what it was.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: And a lock with no keyhole. Letters on it. A name, I think.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud looked at him then, and whatever she had been going to say about weed, she let it go.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Then we're not asking me. Row us in. Your herbalist has a letter he's only read the front page of, and I want to hear the rest of it out loud.
